description.narrative: Tuvalu remains heavily dependent on imported diesel for electricity generation, exposing its population to volatile fuel prices, high electricity costs, and supply disruptions, while contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and undermining national climate goals. The country is also among the most climate-vulnerable globally, with low-lying communities threatened by sea-level rise, extreme weather, and saltwater intrusion.The Tuvalu Rural Electrification Fund (TREF) project will accelerate the transition to a resilient, equitable, and low-emission power system. Its goal is to achieve access to affordable, reliable, renewable electricity while enhancing national capacity, strengthening policies, and building climate resilience in the energy sector.Four interlinked components will: (i) establish and capitalize a national rural electrification fund to pool donor and domestic finance; (ii) design a gender-responsive co-managed delivery model for decentralized minigrids through partnerships between island councils, private providers, and the national utility; (iii) pilot a 100% renewable solar-battery minigrid in Vaitupu and prepare feasibility studies for seven additional outer islands; and (iv) strengthen institutional, regulatory, and workforce capacity with a focus on gender equality.TREF will serve as the national financing and delivery mechanism for outer-island energy systems, establishing a sustainable platform for renewable electrification and lifecycle maintenance. Through the Vaitupu pilot and fund capitalization, the project will create investment-ready packages enabling government and partners to replicate the model across remaining outer islands.This transition will deliver tangible climate and social benefits. Replacing diesel use across Funafuti and the outer islands will avoid 33,855.9 tCO2e over the lifetime of project assets. Direct beneficiaries include 1,007 people (483 women), with 4,030 indirect beneficiaries (1,970 women).
